strings.name: Patricia Espinosa
strings.role: Former Mexican foreign minister; onepoint5 founding partner and CEO
strings.summary: Patricia Espinosa is a Mexican career diplomat and former foreign minister, ambassador and Executive Secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. She chaired the 2010 Cancún climate conference and led the convention's secretariat from 2016 to 2022, supporting international climate cooperation. After leaving office, she became onepoint5's founding partner and CEO, working in strategy and sustainability advisory services and continuing to discuss the energy transition.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. A September 2026 institutional partnership announcement and coverage of a 10 November event support recent activity. UN appointment and arrival in office are distinguished; postgraduate study is not automatically described as a master's or doctorate. Climate targets and project plans are not completed results.
strings.influence.rationale: As Mexico's foreign minister and head of the UN climate convention secretariat, she participated in climate negotiations and implementation of agreements.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Mexico City on 21 October 1958, she holds an international relations degree from El Colegio de México and pursued postgraduate international law studies at Geneva's Graduate Institute. The congressional appointment review records a degree and postgraduate study, without specifically certifying a master's or doctorate.
strings.facts.f2.label: Multilateral diplomatic experience
strings.facts.f2.value: She handled economic affairs at Mexico's permanent mission to the UN in Geneva in 1982–1988. In 2002–2006 she was ambassador to Austria and representative to international organisations in Vienna, also covering relations with Slovakia and Slovenia.
strings.highlights.h1.title: International experience in human rights and gender issues
strings.highlights.h1.text: Elected chair of the UN General Assembly's Third Committee in 1996, she worked on multilateral social, humanitarian and human-rights matters. Chairing this committee is distinct from being General Assembly president and from her later leadership of the climate convention secretariat.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Preparing island energy projects
strings.highlights.h2.text: On 23 September 2026, RMI announced a signed memorandum with onepoint5 establishing an investment platform for island resilience and energy security. The partners planned an initial Pacific focus on project preparation, coordination and finance. Signing and launching the platform do not establish that all projects were funded or built.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Ending her climate-secretariat tenure
strings.timeline.t1.text: The convention's official historical biography gives 16 July as her final day of service. She subsequently became onepoint5's founding partner and CEO. The current company page confirms her role, but is not used to infer a company registration date or her exact starting date.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Second three-year term announced
strings.timeline.t2.text: The secretariat announced her appointment to a second three-year term after communication from the UN secretary-general's office and consultation with the COP Bureau. The date 3 July is the announcement date, not an independently established first day of the new term.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Taking office as UN climate Executive Secretary
strings.timeline.t3.text: Ban Ki-moon appointed her on 18 May; she began work on 18 July, succeeding Christiana Figueres. The Executive Secretary heads the permanent secretariat, a role distinct from COP president. The 2015 Paris Agreement cannot be credited to her as if she already held this office then.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Returning as Mexico's ambassador to Germany
strings.timeline.t4.text: Mexican institutional biographies date this second term to 2013–2016; congressional documents record the 2013 appointment review. Some UN biographies instead give 2012 as the start. The discrepancy is retained, and the review document's date is not treated as the date of presenting credentials.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Cancún conference reaches a package of agreements
strings.timeline.t5.text: COP16, which she chaired, produced the Cancún Agreements covering mitigation, adaptation, technology cooperation and establishment of the Green Climate Fund. These were institutions and goals negotiated among parties, not global emissions cuts or payments already delivered by her personally.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becoming Mexico's foreign minister
strings.timeline.t6.text: She began serving as foreign minister and remained until 30 November 2012, coordinating Mexico's foreign relations and multilateral diplomacy. This was a national government position, distinct from her subsequent international role at the UN secretariat.
strings.timeline.t7.title: First appointment as ambassador to Germany
strings.timeline.t7.text: She first served as Mexico's ambassador to Germany in 2001–2002, before moving to Austria and multilateral posts in Vienna. This initial German posting is separate from her return from 2013.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Joining Mexico's career diplomatic service
strings.timeline.t8.text: The congressional appointment review explicitly records her entry into the Mexican Foreign Service on this date and promotion to ambassadorial rank in January 2000. Diplomatic rank and later assignments to particular countries are separate milestones.
